title: Only You Have I Known: Privilege and Accountability
summary: God tells Israel that because he chose it alone among the families of the earth, he will punish it for all its iniquities. A chain of questions about cause and effect leads to the conclusion that when the LORD has spoken, the prophet must speak. Foreign nations are called to witness the oppression in Samaria, and God announces that an enemy will plunder the city, leaving only scraps, while the altars of Bethel and the fine houses of the rich are torn down.
story: Chapters 1 and 2 ended with Israel's name at the end of a list of guilty nations. Chapter 3 begins the second major section of the book, a series of messages introduced by "Hear this word" (3:1; 4:1; 5:1), and it starts by answering the objection an Israelite would raise: surely God's chosen people are safe. Amos turns that assumption upside down. Election means closer accountability, not immunity. The chapter also explains why Amos, a herdsman with no prophetic credentials, speaks at all: God has roared, and he cannot keep silent.
historical:
Samaria had been the capital of the northern kingdom since King Omri bought the hill and built the city in the early ninth century BC (1 Kings 16:24). It stood on a high, easily defended hill, and its kings had built palaces and fortifications there. In Amos's day, under Jeroboam II (about 793 to 753 BC), it was the center of the kingdom's wealth. The Bible mentions an ivory house built by Ahab (1 Kings 22:39), and excavations at Samaria in the twentieth century recovered many fragments of carved ivory used to decorate furniture and walls, generally dated to the ninth and eighth centuries BC. They give a vivid picture of the luxury Amos saw.

The "enemy" of verse 11 is not named, but within about forty years Assyria besieged Samaria and captured it in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6). Bethel, about ten miles north of Jerusalem, was the royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf about two centuries earlier (1 Kings 12:28-33). Its destruction was completed later by King Josiah of Judah, who tore down the altar at Bethel in the late seventh century BC (2 Kings 23:15).
cultural:
Verse 12 draws on shepherding law. A shepherd who lost an animal to a wild beast could clear himself by bringing the owner what remained of it as proof that it had been killed and not stolen (Exodus 22:13; compare Genesis 31:39). Two legs or a piece of an ear rescued from a lion's mouth would prove that the sheep was gone. Amos applies it grimly: what is "rescued" of Samaria will only prove that the city was destroyed. The last line of verse 12 is difficult Hebrew, and translations differ; it may refer to the edge of a bed and a piece of a couch, fragments of the luxurious furniture the rich lounged on.

The horns of an altar were projections at its four corners. They were the holiest part of the altar, where blood was applied in sacrifice, and a person fleeing for his life could seize them to claim sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50-51). To cut them off is to say that there will be no refuge at Bethel. Wealthy families in the ancient Near East sometimes kept separate houses for the cool rainy season and the hot summer, a mark of great wealth; Amos names both and says both will come down.
literary: The chapter opens with a solemn announcement and a startling turn in verse 2: "Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities." Verses 3 to 8 are a series of rhetorical questions drawn from everyday life (two walking together, a lion's roar, a bird in a snare, a trumpet in a city) that each point to a cause behind an effect. The sequence climbs to the claim that disaster in a city comes from the LORD, and then to its real point: when God speaks, the prophet cannot help prophesying. Verses 9 to 15 take the form of a trial, with foreign nations summoned as witnesses and a sentence pronounced on Samaria and Bethel. The lion image links back to 1:2 and forward to verse 12.

outline.t: Cause and effect: the lion has roared
Bethel's altars and the fine houses torn down

doctrines.note: God's choice of Israel is real ("Only you have I known"), but the covenant is a relationship with obligations, not a guarantee of safety. Privilege brings responsibility, and those who know God most closely will answer to him most strictly.

Verse 7 says that the Lord does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets. God's judgments are not random; he warns before he acts, and the prophet is the means by which he speaks.
Verse 6 attributes calamity in a city to the LORD. Amos insists that God rules over history, including its disasters, so that nothing that falls on Israel is outside his hand or without meaning.

words.note: Yada, to know. Here it means more than awareness: it is the knowing of close relationship and choice, as when God says he knew Jeremiah before he formed him (Jeremiah 1:5). God "knew" Israel in this committed, covenant sense, which is exactly why its unfaithfulness matters so much.

Sod, counsel, council, or secret plan. It can describe a circle of close advisers and the plans discussed there. In verse 7 God reveals his sod to the prophets, admitting them, as it were, into his council, which gives their words their authority.

Ashuq, oppression, from a verb meaning to wrong, extort, or exploit. Amos calls foreign nations to look at the "acts of oppression" inside Samaria. Even outsiders, he implies, would be shocked by what goes on in the capital of God's people.

Shen, tooth, and by extension ivory. The "houses of ivory" were buildings decorated with carved ivory inlays, costly imports that signaled wealth and status. Ivory fragments from Samaria give material evidence of the luxury Amos condemns.

christ: Amos's principle that greater privilege brings greater accountability is echoed by Jesus: "From everyone who has been given much, much will be required" (Luke 12:48). Jesus also warned towns that had seen his miracles that they would face a stricter judgment than Tyre and Sidon (Matthew 11:20-24), which is Amos's logic applied to those who met God in person. At the same time, the chapter's claim that God reveals his plans to his servants the prophets reaches its fullness in Christ. Hebrews opens by saying that God, who spoke in the past through the prophets, has spoken in these last days by his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). In Jesus, God does not merely reveal his plan but carries it out.

hard.q: Does verse 6 mean that God causes every disaster?
hard.a: Verse 6 asks, "If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?" The Hebrew word for calamity is the common word for evil or harm, which is why some older translations read it as evil. The context is judgment on a rebellious nation, and Amos's point is that Israel should not read its coming disaster as chance or as the work of other gods. It is the LORD's doing, and it carries a message. Many theologians see here a statement of God's sovereignty over history, including suffering, without making God the author of moral evil; human agents like Assyria remain responsible for their cruelty. Others stress that the verse is specific to a covenant setting and should not be turned into a general rule that every disaster is a punishment, which Scripture elsewhere resists (Job; Luke 13:1-5). What the verse does teach clearly is that God is not absent from catastrophe, and that his people should listen for what he is saying through it.

questions: God chose Israel and therefore will punish it (verse 2). How does being close to God raise the stakes of how we live, rather than lowering them?
Amos says he cannot help speaking because the Lord has spoken. When have you felt compelled to say something true that others did not want to hear?
Foreign nations are summoned to witness the oppression in Samaria. How might outsiders see the failures of God's people more clearly than insiders do?
